# Field

The label, helper text, message and validation state around a form control.

```tsx
import { Field } from "@rata/react";
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `field` |
| Family | inputs |
| Tier | free |
| Status (css / react / figma) | latest / latest / future |
| Depends on | `visually-hidden` |

## Behavior

Owns everything around a form control — the label, the required marker, the helper text, the message, and the `data-status` the control's own CSS selects on. Built on `getFieldProps`, which derives every id from the field's own and is the same primitive `TextField` has always used.

Headless contract: `getFieldProps` in `packages/primitives/src/field.ts` — importable from `@rata/primitives` without the React wrapper or any CSS.

- **The control arrives as a function, not as children** — Field has to hand the control its `id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-required`, `aria-disabled` and `readOnly`. Of the three ways to do that, cloning `children` breaks the moment someone wraps their input in a fragment or a div; a context the control opts into makes a control rendered OUTSIDE a Field silently unlabelled, which is the failure this component exists to prevent. A function makes the wiring visible at the call site, works for a control from another library, and cannot be forgotten — there is nothing to render without it.
- **It does not style the control's box** — Height, inline padding, border and focus ring stay with each control, because they genuinely differ: a textarea grows with its content, a select reserves a well for its chevron, a checkbox is square and small. Field owning them would mean every control overriding them. What Field owns is what is identical across all of them — which is everything outside the box.
- **`status` lives here rather than on the control** — It drives `data-status` on the root, and each control's stylesheet selects on that for its own ring. One state, read by many controls, set in one place — and it is also what decides whether the message joins the description chain, which is an accessibility fact about the group rather than about the input.
- **`TextField` keeps its flat API and is rebuilt on this, not replaced by it** — `<TextField label="Email" />` stays one element with one prop — a component whose commonest use got more verbose to serve an abstraction would be a bad trade. Field is what TextField is made of. Callers reach for Field directly for the controls that have no wrapper yet and for third-party ones; everything else keeps the shorthand.
- **The primitive is renamed `getFieldProps`, with the old name kept as an alias** — It was called `getTextFieldProps`, and nothing in it has ever been about text: it returns `root`, `label`, `input`, `description` and `message` bags containing ids and ARIA, and a `<select>` or `<textarea>` could consume it unchanged today. A Select built on something called `getTextFieldProps` would be the lookup surface lying about itself. `getTextFieldProps` and `TextFieldStatus` continue to be exported as aliases so nothing outside this repo breaks.
- **`disabled` is `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, never the native attribute** — This system's rule, and for an input `readOnly` is the analogue of the button's click guard: it blocks editing while keeping the control in the tab order and the accessibility tree. Note the consequence, which is the same one `TextField`'s contract already carries — a readOnly field still submits its value.
- **`labelHidden` hides the pixels, never the label** — The label element is still rendered and still bound by `for`, so nothing about the accessible name changes. The alternative people reach for — dropping the label and letting `placeholder` stand in — loses the name on the first keystroke, which is when the reader most needs it.

## Props

Extends `Omit<HTMLAttributes<HTMLDivElement>, "children">`.

| Prop | Type | Default | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `label` | `ReactNode` | — | The control's name. |
| `children` | `(control: FieldControlProps) => ReactNode` | — | Renders the control, given the id and ARIA it must carry. |
| `labelHidden?` | `boolean` | — | Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree. |
| `id?` | `string` | — | Stable id for the control, when something outside needs to point at it. |
| `status?` | `FieldStatus` | `"idle"` | Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the control's ring. |
| `description?` | `ReactNode` | — | Persistent helper text under the control. |
| `message?` | `ReactNode` | — | The status-dependent line: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note. |
| `required?` | `boolean` | — | Marks the field required, in the label and to assistive technology. |
| `disabled?` | `boolean` | — | Blocks editing while keeping the field focusable, readable and announced. |
| `className?` | `string` | — | Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle. |

### `label`

```ts
label: ReactNode
```

The control's name.

Source doc: The control's name. Always required — `labelHidden` hides it, nothing removes it.

**Use when**

- A short noun phrase: "Billing email", not "Enter your billing email".

**Don't use for**

- Leaving it out for a field whose purpose looks obvious. There is no unlabelled option — `labelHidden` is how a visually bare field is built.

**Accessibility** Bound to the control with `for`/`id` by the primitive, so it is the accessible name and clicking it focuses the control.

### `children`

```ts
children: (control: FieldControlProps) => ReactNode
```

Renders the control, given the id and ARIA it must carry.

**Use when**

- Spreading the argument onto the control and nothing else: `{(control) => <select {...control} />}`.
- Wrapping a control this system does not own yet, which is the case Field exists for outside its own components.

**Don't use for**

- Dropping the argument. A control rendered without it has no id, no accessible name and no description chain — and it will look correct, which is what makes it worth saying.

**Accessibility** The argument carries `id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `aria-required`, `aria-disabled` and `readOnly`. Every one of them is derived, so none can drift from the label and message beside it.

### `labelHidden`

```ts
labelHidden?: boolean
```

Takes the label off screen while leaving it in the accessibility tree.

**Use when**

- A field whose meaning is already carried by its surroundings — a search box under a heading that names it.

**Don't use for**

- Using it and then relying on `placeholder` to carry the name. The placeholder disappears on the first keystroke.

**Accessibility** The label element is still rendered and still bound. Nothing about the accessible name changes — only the pixels.

### `id`

```ts
id?: string
```

Stable id for the control, when something outside needs to point at it.

Source doc: Stable id for the control. Defaults to a generated one.

**Use when**

- A form library that addresses fields by id, or an external error summary linking to the field it describes.

**Don't use for**

- Reusing one across two fields. Every id under it — description, message — is derived from this, so a duplicate silently crosses two fields' wiring.

### `status`

```ts
status?: FieldStatus = "idle"
```

Validation lifecycle, driving the message tone, `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy` and the control's ring.

Source doc: Validation lifecycle. Drives `aria-invalid`, `aria-busy`, and the control's ring.

**Use when**

- `validating` for an in-flight check, such as a uniqueness lookup.
- `invalid` with a `message` saying what to do about it.

**Don't use for**

- `invalid` with no message. The ring says something is wrong and the colour says it twice; only the message says what.

**Accessibility** `invalid` sets `aria-invalid` and pulls the message into `aria-describedby`; `validating` sets `aria-busy`. While `idle` the message stays on the page but leaves the description chain, so a stale message is not announced.

### `description`

```ts
description?: ReactNode
```

Persistent helper text under the control.

**Use when**

- A constraint the reader needs before they type: a format, a limit, where the value ends up.

**Don't use for**

- Repeating the label in a sentence. It is read out after the name, so a restatement is heard twice.

**Accessibility** Joins `aria-describedby` ahead of the message, so a constraint is heard before a failure.

### `message`

```ts
message?: ReactNode
```

The status-dependent line: the error, the confirmation, or the in-flight note.

Source doc: Status-dependent message under the control: the error, confirmation, or in-flight note.

**Use when**

- What to do about an `invalid` status, in the imperative: "Check this number."

**Don't use for**

- Putting the permanent constraint here. It vanishes from the description chain whenever the status returns to idle — that is `description`.

**Accessibility** Announced politely rather than as an alert: it is already in `aria-describedby`, and an assertive region would announce it a second time when focus lands.

### `required`

```ts
required?: boolean
```

Marks the field required, in the label and to assistive technology.

Source doc: Marks the field required to assistive technology and in the label.

**Use when**

- Fields that genuinely block submission. On a form where nearly everything is required, mark the optional ones instead.

**Don't use for**

- Pairing it with a hand-written asterisk in `label`. This renders one, and the second would be read out.

**Accessibility** `aria-required` on the control. The rendered asterisk is `aria-hidden`, because announcing it too would say the requirement twice.

### `disabled`

```ts
disabled?: boolean
```

Blocks editing while keeping the field focusable, readable and announced.

**Use when**

- A field whose value is decided elsewhere and should still be readable.

**Don't use for**

- Assuming the value is withheld. `readOnly` still submits — if the value must not reach the server, do not render the field.

**Accessibility** `aria-disabled` plus `readOnly`, never the native attribute, so the field stays in the tab order and the accessibility tree.

### `className`

```ts
className?: string
```

Class for the wrapper — the width the form wants, not a restyle.

**Use when**

- The measure or grid placement the form decides, which this component deliberately does not own.

**Don't use for**

- Restyling the label or message. Those come from the type scale, and a hand-written size drifts the moment the seed moves.

## Use cases

### A control this system does not wrap yet

The case Field exists for: a native control with no component of its own.

```tsx
<Field label="Country" description="Where the order ships.">
  {(control) => (
    <select {...control}>
      <option>Sri Lanka</option>
    </select>
  )}
</Field>
```

The argument is spread onto the control and nowhere else. Everything the reader hears — the name, the helper text, the requirement — is wired from it.

### A field that failed validation

Reporting what went wrong, where the reader can act on it.

```tsx
<Field label="Card number" status="invalid" message="Check this number." required>
  {(control) => <input {...control} inputMode="numeric" />}
</Field>
```

The ring, the colour and the message say it three ways, and only the message says what to do. `status` also decides that the message joins the description chain — while idle it stays on the page and leaves the chain, so a stale error is not announced.

### A third-party control given the system's treatment

A date picker or combobox from another library, which should still look and announce like every other field.

```tsx
<Field label="Departure" description="Any date after today.">
  {(control) => <ThirdPartyDatePicker {...control} />}
</Field>
```

Field styles nothing inside the control, which is what makes this work — it owns the label, the helper text and the state, and leaves the box alone.

### Reaching for the wrong component

The control already has a wrapper of its own.

```tsx
<Field label="Email">
  {(control) => <TextField label="Email" {...control} />}
</Field>
```

Don't. `TextField` is built on Field and renders its own label, so this produces two labels and two ids for one input. `<TextField label="Email" />` is the whole thing — reach for Field only where no wrapper exists.

## Token recipe

### base

A column. The gap is the only measurement here, and it is deliberately tighter than it looks it should be.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| display | `flex, column` |
| gap | `space.stack.2xs — not space.stack.xs: the label and the helper text each carry their own line-height leading, so the perceived gap is already larger than the number, and the next step up reads as separation rather than as grouping` |

### label

The control's name, at the label role of the type scale.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| colour | `theme.fg.primary` |
| font-size | `type.label.size` |
| font-weight | `type.label.weight` |
| line-height | `type.label.line-height` |

### required-marker

The asterisk. Required-ness is information, not a fault, so it is not the danger tone.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| colour | `theme.fg.secondary` |

### description

Persistent helper text, and always ahead of the message in the description order so a constraint is heard before a failure.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| margin | `space.0` |
| colour | `theme.fg.secondary` |
| font-size | `type.supporting.size` |
| line-height | `type.supporting.line-height` |

### message

The status-dependent line. Neutral until the status says otherwise, so a field that has not been judged does not look judged.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| margin | `space.0` |
| colour | `theme.fg.secondary` |
| font-size | `type.supporting.size` |
| line-height | `type.supporting.line-height` |
| when invalid | `theme.danger-role.fg — the role's text colour on the page background, never its saturated bg, which is a non-text indicator tone` |

### disabled

Dimmed as a whole rather than removed, because the control underneath stays focusable and readable.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| opacity | `state.disabled-opacity, on the root so the label and helper text dim with the control` |
